entities.summary:
Guy of Avesnes, who served as the Bishop of Utrecht from 1301 until his death on June 6, 1317, was a significant political and ecclesiastical figure in the turbulent Low Countries during the early 14th century. Born into the powerful House of Avesnes, as the son of John II, Count of Holland and Hainaut, and Philippa of Luxembourg, his episcopacy was inextricably linked to the intricate dynastic rivalries and burgeoning urban independence movements of the era. He represents a pivotal moment in the decline of the temporal power of the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht, caught between the ambitions of his own family and the increasing autonomy of the region's cities.

His tenure as bishop was largely defined by a struggle to maintain the authority and territorial integrity of the Prince-Bishopric against formidable external and internal pressures. Most notably, Guy found himself in frequent conflict with his own brother, William III, Count of Holland and Hainaut, over strategic territories and influence within the diocese, particularly the Sticht of Utrecht. These conflicts often devolved into military skirmishes and political maneuvering, draining the episcopal coffers and further entrenching the power of the Counts of Holland in areas historically under Utrecht's suzerainty. He also grappled with the growing assertiveness of the city of Utrecht, which sought greater self-governance and economic liberties, challenging the traditional feudal prerogatives of the bishop.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Guy of Avesnes's episcopacy significantly weakened the temporal power of the Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht, contributing to its eventual absorption into larger regional states and altering the political landscape of the Low Countries.
